event: Elsie wakes in the hay with Cora's hand still in hers, and Cora asleep, her bun come loose.
prose: Elsie woke to grey light in the little square window and the smell of hay. A cockerel was going somewhere below, and the sheep had begun to shift and complain in the folds. She lay where she was, warm, and for a moment could not feel her left hand, and then could. It was still held. Cora's fingers were still wound through hers under the blanket, loose now with sleep, but there. Cora was asleep. She lay on her side, turned in toward Elsie in the night, and her bun had come loose. Half of it had slid down onto the hay, and a long black rope of hair lay over her shoulder and across the blanket, nearly to Elsie's wrist.

pictured.coverAfter: Elsie woke to grey light in the little square window and the smell
pictured.outfit: charcoal coat, bun come loose, hair half down

event: Elsie lies still and looks at Cora's sleeping face, all its guard gone.
prose: Elsie lay very still so as not to wake her, and looked. She had not seen Cora's face without its guard on before. Asleep, it had none. The straight dark brows had come apart. The mouth that stayed pressed flat all day had fallen a little open, soft and pink, and Elsie could hear the small even breath going in and out of it. There was a wisp of hay caught in her lashes and a crease in her cheek from the blanket's hem. She looked younger, and so lovely that Elsie's chest went tight and warm, the way it went at a sunrise, and she wanted, absurdly, to put her thumb on the crease and smooth it out. She didn't. She only lay and looked, and held the hand.

event: Cora wakes, sees their hands, and takes hers back as if from a stove.
prose: Cora's lashes moved. Her eyes opened, grey and unfocused, and looked straight into Elsie's from a hand's breadth away. For a moment she only looked, soft and drowsy, and something at the corner of her mouth began to turn up. Then her eyes went down, to the blanket, to where their two hands lay twined together on the hay between them. Cora took hers back. She took it back so fast that the blanket jumped, the way a hand comes off a stove it hadn't known was lit, and held it against her own chest in a fist. "Good morning," Elsie whispered, smiling. Cora's face had gone white, then pink, high on the cheekbones. She didn't answer.

event: Cora is down the ladder pinning up her hair before anyone else stirs.
prose: She was up before Elsie could say anything else. She got out from under the blanket in one long careful movement, without touching anyone, and went across the hay on her knees to the square hole of the ladder. Elsie heard her boots find the rungs. She rolled onto her elbow and looked down through the hatch. In the yard below, in the grey light by the sheepfolds, Cora stood with her back to the barn and her hands up behind her head and a mouthful of hairpins between her lips. She was twisting the long black rope of her hair up and round and pinning it, hard, pin after pin, until there wasn't a strand loose. Behind Elsie, Tamsin and Tilly slept on.

event: Tamsin wakes with hay in her curls; Tilly wakes with hay everywhere.
prose: Tamsin woke half an hour later with a great creaking yawn that Elsie felt all down her own back. She sat up. There was hay in her copper curls, a great deal of it, stuck through them like straw through a nest, and she blinked at Elsie out of the middle of it, green-eyed and slow and grinning. "Morning," she said, hoarse. At the far end of the row Tilly sat up too, all at once, like a jack out of a box. Tilly had hay everywhere. It was in her braids and her collar and her ears, down the front of her blouse, stuck to the soot on her cheek. One long stalk stood straight up out of her hair like a feather. "What," said Tilly, and sneezed.

event: At the well Elsie tells everyone cheerfully that Cora held her hand all night, and it was cold.
prose: The well stood in the middle of the yard, with a stone lip and a bucket on a rope. Cora was already there, washing her face, her hair pinned and her coat buttoned to the throat. Elsie came down the ladder and across to her, picking hay off her skirt, with Tamsin and Tilly yawning behind. Tamsin began to wind the bucket up. "Did everyone sleep?" Elsie asked happily. "I slept so well. It was so warm. Cora held my hand all night," she added, to all of them, the way she'd have said it had rained. "Didn't you, Cora? All night long. And your hand was cold as anything, the whole time. Even under the blanket."

event: Tamsin drops the bucket; Tilly goes very still; Cora turns scarlet to the collar.
prose: Tamsin let go of the handle. The bucket went down the well, rattling and banging off the stones all the way, and hit the water far below with a great hollow splash. Tamsin didn't go after it. She stood with her hands still up where the handle had been and stared at Cora. Tilly had gone very still, with a stalk of hay halfway out of her braid between her finger and thumb. And Cora turned scarlet. It came up out of her collar and went all the way up her neck and over her face to her hairline, a deep, painful, burning red, and she stood in it with her wet hands at her sides and didn't look at anyone.

event: Elsie says she'll knit Cora gloves, and wonders why everyone has gone so quiet.
prose: "I'm going to knit you some gloves," Elsie told her warmly. "Proper ones, wool, for your cold hands. My mother taught me. I can do fingers and everything." She smiled at Cora. Cora looked at the well. Elsie looked round at the others. Tamsin was looking at Cora. Tilly was looking at her own boots. The yard had gone so quiet that Elsie could hear a sheep chewing on the far side of the fold wall. She didn't understand it. It was only gloves. "I'd like to," she said, a little less sure. "If you'd wear them." Tamsin made a sound in her throat and went to fish for the bucket.

event: The headwoman brings porridge, and says the trolls fished all night and took no sheep.
prose: The headwoman came across the yard with a pot of porridge on her hip, four wooden bowls stacked in her other hand and her crook hooked over her arm. She set the pot on the well's lip and began to ladle. It was thick and grey and hot, with a puddle of honey in the middle of each bowl. "I was up," she said, handing Elsie hers. "Sat at my door half the night with a lantern, watching the bridge." She ladled Tamsin's. "Fished. The pair of them. Fished all night in that pool, splashing about like children." She banged the ladle on the pot. "Counted my folds at first light. Not a sheep gone. Not one." She sounded almost put out about it.

event: Down at the bridge the young troll waves to Tilly from the pool; the mother only watches.
prose: They went down to the bridge with their bowls to say goodbye. The pool under the arch was deep and clear and green, and the young troll was sitting in it up to his chest, with the morning sun on his mossy shoulders. He saw them on the bank. He saw Tilly. His great grey arm came up out of the water, streaming, and waved at her, slowly, side to side, the same big clumsy wave as last night. Tilly waved back with her spoon. Out in the deep middle of the pool his mother stood up to her waist, still as a stone. She didn't wave. She watched them a long time with her small dark eyes, and then bent her head to the water again.

event: They start back south along the Wend in the morning sun.
prose: They set off south along the Wend with the sun coming up warm on their left and the meadows steaming. The river ran beside them quick and clear, talking over its stones, and Elsie kept looking at it, the way a person keeps looking at a mended thing to be sure it holds. The sheep watched them go. The headwoman stood at the top of the bank with her crook until they were round the first bend, and when Elsie turned to wave, she lifted the crook, once. Tamsin swung Margery up onto her shoulder. Tilly picked hay out of her collar as she walked, stalk by stalk, and dropped it behind her on the path.

event: Tamsin walks close to Elsie and says, low, that she'd hold Elsie's hand too, if it's cold.
prose: After a while Tamsin dropped back to walk beside Elsie. She walked close, closer than the path needed, so that her bare arm brushed Elsie's shoulder with every step, warm from the sun. She was quiet for a bit, which wasn't like her. Ahead of them Tilly was telling Cora something about silt. Then Tamsin bent her head and spoke, low, just for Elsie, with her eyes on the path. "I'd hold your hand too," she said. "If it's cold." She cleared her throat. "Your hand. If it gets cold. I've got warm hands." She held one up and looked at it, as if to check. "Hot, mostly. Ask anyone."

event: Elsie gives her hand at once, and Tamsin holds it all the way to the next stile.
prose: Elsie gave her hand at once. She didn't have to think about it; she slipped it into Tamsin's, laced their fingers together and swung them, smiling up at her. "It isn't cold," she said. "But I'd like that." Tamsin's hand closed round hers. It was warm, as promised, and hard with calluses from Margery's haft, and it held on firmly, as if Elsie might be taken back. Tamsin's thumb moved once over her knuckles, slowly, and then lay still. She didn't look at Elsie. She looked straight ahead up the path, and her ears had gone red under her curls, and she didn't let go until they reached the next stile, where she had to.

changes.note: Bond: Tamsin 60 → 62 (confidence: asks to hold Elsie's hand, and is given it)

event: Elsie takes out her notebook and asks Tilly her favourite things, for Tilly's page.
prose: By the middle of the morning the hills were behind them and the meadows wide and flat. Elsie took her notebook out of her satchel and walked with it open, turning the pages until she found one with only a name at the top. TILLY, it said, in her round careful hand, and under it a great empty space. She licked her pencil. "Tilly," she said, falling into step beside her. "I need your favourite things. For your page. I've got a page for everyone I love, look, and yours is empty. It's a disgrace. What are your favourite things?"

changes.note: Bond: Tilly 47 → 48 (kindness: Elsie asks her favourite things for her page)

event: Tilly lists pear fizz, blue flames and the smell of sulphur, then goes red and stops.
prose: Tilly lit up. "Oh! Oh, um. Pear fizz," she said, counting on her fingers at once. "Mine, not the shop one, the shop one's too sweet. And blue flames. The steady kind, with no wick, when they stand up straight and don't flicker and you can see right through the bottom of them. And the smell of sulphur." She said it fast and happily. "And the smell of—" She stopped. She stopped dead, with her mouth open and her fourth finger up. Her face went red, a slow red that started at her collar and filled her up like a glass, all the way to her hairline. She shut her mouth.

event: Elsie asks what the last one was; Tilly says it's a secret and walks faster.
prose: "The smell of what?" Elsie asked, pencil ready. "I've got sulphur. What was the last one?" "It's a secret," said Tilly. She said it very high. "It's a secret, it's not a thing, it's not anything, you can't write it down." She put her hand flat over Elsie's notebook, as if Elsie might write it anyway, then snatched it off again as if the paper were hot. And she walked faster. She walked so fast that her braids bounced, all the way up to the front, past Tamsin, until she was ahead of everyone with her ears pink and her back very straight. Elsie looked at the page. She wrote pear fizz, and blue flames, and sulphur, and then, after a moment, a small question mark.

event: Elsie asks Cora hers; Cora says tea, black, one sugar, as Elsie already knows.
prose: Cora was walking a little apart, on the river side, with her ledger under her arm. Elsie turned to a fresh page, wrote CORA at the top of it and fell into step with her. "Cora," she said. "Your turn. What are your favourite things?" Cora looked at the page, and at her own name on it. She looked ahead again. "Tea," she said. "Black. Strong. One sugar." She said it as if reading out an entry. "As you know perfectly well, Fairweather. You've made it me often enough." Elsie laughed. "I know. I'm writing it anyway. It's the rule. What else?"

event: Elsie waits, and Cora adds, very quietly: and lavender.
prose: Cora didn't answer. Elsie waited. She walked beside her with her pencil over the page and waited, the way she waited for a shy child at a caravan stop, without hurrying her, and the river went by, and a lark went up. They walked a long way like that. Then Cora spoke, so quietly that Elsie nearly lost it under the river. "And lavender," Cora said. She didn't look round. Elsie looked up at her, and breathed in, and there it was, faint, under the ink, in the charcoal wool of the coat beside her: lavender. "Oh," she said softly, delighted. "That's why your coat smells of it." Cora's step faltered, just once. Elsie wrote it down.

event: They come in through the north gate, and the gate clerk logs them in with a grin.
prose: They came in through the north gate in the late morning. The same clerk sat in the window of the little gatehouse with the same mug and the big chained ledger open in front of him. He saw them coming up the road and put the mug down. He was grinning before they reached him. "Fairweather party," he said, and wrote it without being asked, and spelled it right. "Four, in. Back from the toll bridge." He looked up at Elsie from under his eyebrows. "Heard about you," he said, still grinning. "Shepherd's lad came down at dawn with a cart of fleeces. Talking to trolls." He turned the ledger round for Cora to sign, and shook his head, and laughed into his tea.

event: At the guild hall the talk stops when they walk in, then starts up again louder.
prose: The guild hall was full, as it was most mornings before noon: adventurers all along the quest board, a queue at the clerk's desk, the smell of wet leather and ink and somebody's breakfast. Elsie pushed open the big door and walked in with the others behind her. The talk stopped. It stopped all down the hall, table by table, head by head, like a wave going out, until the great timber room was silent and every face in it was turned toward the door. Elsie stopped too, startled, on the threshold. Then, all at once, the talk started up again, louder than before, a great rush of it, every voice going at once.

event: Two adventurers at the board say troll, and bargain, and Enthraller, and one raises his mug.
prose: Elsie caught pieces of it as they went in. Two adventurers stood by the E-rank end of the board, a big bearded man in mail and a woman with a bow across her back, their heads together. "—troll," the woman was saying, "under the bridge, and she just—" "A bargain," said the man. "With a troll. A bargain." "The Enthraller," said the woman, and looked up straight at Elsie, and stopped. The man looked too. He had a mug in his hand. He looked at Elsie a moment longer, at her pink hair and her muddy boots, and then he raised his mug to her, gravely, the way adventurers raise them to each other across a tavern, and drank.

event: A clerk meets them at the door: the guildmaster wants Elsie and Cora upstairs now.
prose: A clerk was already coming through the crowd toward them, a thin young woman with ink on her fingers and a pen behind her ear. She stopped in front of Elsie and Cora and looked from one to the other, a little out of breath. "The guildmaster wants you," she said. "Both of you. Upstairs. Now, she said." She glanced at Tamsin and Tilly. "Just the Enthraller and the Warden." Elsie's stomach gave a small turn. She looked at Cora. Cora's face had gone smooth and still and correct, the face she wore for the guild, and she tucked her ledger under her arm and nodded once. "Of course," Cora said.

event: Tamsin and Tilly wait by the board while Elsie and Cora go up.
prose: Tamsin put a hand on Elsie's shoulder and squeezed. "We'll be by the board," she said. "Right there. Go on." Tilly nodded hard, her eyes huge, and then, because she couldn't think what else to do, hugged Elsie quickly round the middle and let go. Elsie followed the clerk and Cora up the wide wooden stairs at the back of the hall. Halfway up she looked back over the rail. Tamsin and Tilly were standing by the quest board side by side, Tamsin with her arms folded and Margery leaning on the wall beside her, Tilly twisting a braid round and round her finger, both of them watching the stairs.

event: The guildmaster has heard of the toll bridge already, and waves them to chairs.
prose: The guildmaster's office was a long room under the roof, with a window over Brightwater Square and a sword on the wall above the hearth, old and plain and well kept. The guildmaster sat behind a desk heaped with paper. She was a broad grey-haired woman in her fifties, with a swordswoman's shoulders and big weathered hands, and she looked up as they came in. "The old toll bridge," she said. It wasn't a question. "I've had the shepherds' runner, the gate clerk's tally and half my hall in here gossiping since dawn." She waved one big hand at two chairs in front of the desk. "Sit."

pictured.coverAfter: The guildmaster's office was a long room under the roof, with a window

event: She asks Elsie to tell her plainly what happened at the toll bridge.
prose: They sat. Cora sat the way she stood, straight, her ledger flat on her knees. Elsie sat on the edge of her chair with her hands clasped tight in her lap. The guildmaster leaned back and looked at her for a while, the way a buyer looks over a horse, not unkindly. "Now," she said. "I've heard it from everyone but you, and everyone tells it different. Tell me what happened at the toll bridge, Fairweather. Plainly. Not the way the Heron's telling it. The way it happened." She folded her hands on her stomach. "Take as long as you like."

event: Elsie tells her: the hunger, the silted pools, the weir, the trout.
prose: So Elsie told her. She told it the way it had happened, in order, because she didn't know how to tell it any other way. The headwoman, and the sheep, one a night. The brown pools, silted so shallow she could see the bottom, and the boys who couldn't find a trout. The trolls asleep under the arch. Tilly saying the river was too slow. The troll saying fish, gone, and water, stopped, and pointing. The weir, and the jam, and the drowned cart, and Tilly's bang. The river coming down clean. "And at dusk she caught a trout," Elsie finished, "and gave it to her son. And then she nodded at me." Her eyes stung, telling it. She blinked.

event: The guildmaster asks why she didn't let the Berserker kill them asleep.
prose: The guildmaster was quiet a moment. Then she leaned forward and put her elbows on the desk. "You had a Berserker with you," she said. "Reyes. A good axe, I'm told, when she's herself. And two trolls asleep in the shallows, on a notice that says remove them." She looked at Elsie with pale, hard eyes. "Reyes could have had the big one's head off before it woke. That's how it's done. That's how it's been done on that notice for as long as there've been notices." She tapped the desk with one finger. "Why didn't you let her?"

event: Elsie says nobody had asked the trolls anything yet, and she wanted to ask.
prose: Elsie thought about it. She wanted to give the right answer, and found she only had the true one. "Because they hadn't been asked anything yet," she said. She heard how simple it sounded and went pink, but went on. "Everyone knew what the trolls were doing. Not why. Not the headwoman, not the books. And it seemed—" She spread her hands. "It seemed like a thing you ought to find out first. Before. Because after, you can't." She looked at the guildmaster. "I wanted to ask them. That's all. So I did."

event: The guildmaster looks at Cora; Cora reads her ledger aloud and says that is exactly what she saw.
prose: The guildmaster looked at Cora. She didn't say anything; she only looked, with her grey brows raised. Cora opened her ledger. She turned to a page near the end, and Elsie saw the small exact writing going on and on, over that page and the next. Cora read it aloud. She read in her even guild voice, without hurrying, every line: the sleeping trolls, the Berserker's axe, the Enthraller's hand on its haft. The Enthraller between the troll and its child with her arms out. Skills used, none. The question. The answer. Cora closed the ledger. "That is what I saw, Guildmaster," she said. "Exactly that." Elsie looked at her, and her heart swelled up warm and full.

changes.note: Bond: Cora 37 → 39 (stand: her ledger read aloud speaks for Elsie)

event: The guildmaster asks Elsie what she wants from the guild.
prose: The guildmaster sat back. She looked at Cora for a long moment, then at Elsie, and her mouth did something at one corner that wasn't quite anything yet. "Well," she said. She picked up a pen and put it down again. "Then let me ask you something else, Fairweather, since you like questions. You're an Enthraller on my books. E-rank inside a week, and the whole hall in an uproar over you. Half of them think you'll be the end of us, and the other half want to buy you a drink." She folded her arms. "What is it you want from the guild? What are you after?"

event: Elsie says a blue-doored house on Willow Canal, for all her friends, and the guildmaster laughs.
prose: Elsie didn't have to think about that either. "A house," she said. "There's one on Willow Canal with a blue door. It's to let. It's got a garden gone all wild, and a kitchen big enough for everyone, and a shed for Tilly's still, and I want to live in it with all my friends." She smiled. "That's what I'm saving for. That's what I want." The guildmaster stared at her. Then she laughed. It burst out of her, a great short bark of a laugh that seemed to take her by surprise, and she put her hand over her eyes and laughed into it, her broad shoulders shaking.

event: The guildmaster says that's more than most adventurers ask for, and less than they should.
prose: When she took her hand away she was still smiling, and the smile changed her whole face; it made her look like somebody's aunt. "A house with a blue door," she said. "For your friends." She shook her head. "Do you know what adventurers ask the guild for, when I ask them that? Rank. Gold. Their names on a board. A dungeon all to themselves." She looked at Elsie. "A house is more than most of them ask for, Fairweather," she said. "And a good deal less than they should."

event: She says the city is talking, not all kindly: an Enthraller who talks to trolls frightens some more.
prose: Then the smile went, slowly, and she leaned forward again. "Listen to me," she said. "The city's talking about you. You'll have heard it downstairs. Not all of it's kind." She picked a letter off the heap and put it down again without reading it, as if she knew what it said. "There are folk in this city who still remember the War of Strings. An Enthraller who takes, they understand. They've built a memorial to one." She looked at Elsie steadily. "An Enthraller who talks to trolls frightens some of them more."

event: Elsie asks why; the guildmaster says, because it works.
prose: Elsie frowned. "But why?" she asked. "Why more? I didn't do anything to the trolls. I didn't use anything. Cora wrote it down." She looked at Cora, who was looking at her hands. "I only talked to them." The guildmaster looked at her a long time. "Because it works," she said quietly. "That's why. A thing that takes, folk can fight. They know where its edges are. A thing that asks, and gets a yes out of a river troll—" she spread her hands flat on the desk, "—they can't see where that stops."

event: She tells Cora to go on writing every line, and sends them down.
prose: She turned to Cora. "Warden Vane." Cora sat up straighter, if that was possible. "Keep writing. Every line, the way you read it me just now. Every skill, and every none." The guildmaster tapped the ledger on Cora's knees with one thick finger. "If the day comes that I have to stand up in front of the council with this girl, I want that book in my hand." She sat back and waved them at the door. "Go on. Down you go, the pair of you. And Fairweather," she added, as Elsie got up, "good luck with your house."

event: On the stairs Cora says it's the first time she has heard the guildmaster laugh.
prose: On the stairs, halfway down, Cora stopped. Elsie stopped a step below and looked up at her. Cora stood with one hand on the rail and her ledger held against her chest, looking at the wall with a strange, far-off look on her face. "She laughed," Cora said. "Three years I've reported to that woman, Fairweather. I'd not heard her laugh till today." Elsie beamed. "She's got a lovely laugh," she said. "Hasn't she? Like a dog barking." And Cora's mouth twitched, at one corner, before she could stop it.

event: Downstairs Tamsin and Tilly pounce on them for news.
prose: Tamsin and Tilly were on them before they reached the bottom stair. "Well?" Tamsin demanded, grabbing Elsie's arm. "What did she want? Are you in trouble? Is Cora in trouble? Do I need to hit anyone?" "Are we being thrown out?" Tilly said, at the same time, hanging off Elsie's other arm. "Is it the bang? It was the bang, wasn't it. It was a very big bang. I can pay for the cart. I can't pay for the cart. I can pay for some of the cart—" Elsie laughed and took a hand of each. "Nobody's in trouble," she said.

event: Elsie says the guildmaster laughed about the house, and Tamsin says that's a good sign.
prose: "She asked me what I wanted," Elsie told them, "so I told her about the house. The blue door. And she laughed." She was still pleased about it. "She laughed and laughed, with her hand over her eyes." Tamsin stared at her. Then she grinned, slow and crooked, and let go of Elsie's arm to thump her lightly on the shoulder. "The guildmaster laughed," she said. "At you. Elsie, that's good. That's a good sign. I've stood in that office twice to be told off, and she didn't so much as smile." She looked at Cora, who was looking at the floor. "That's a very good sign," Tamsin said.

event: On the E-rank board are wolves on the north road, Bellmoor barrow, and bandits at Hollin Ford.
prose: They went to the board. The E-rank notices hung at the far end, fewer than the F and further apart, on better paper. Elsie's tag clinked at her belt as she went up on her toes to read them. There were three. Wolves out of the Glasswood on the north road, and a carter's pony taken. Lights and singing at Bellmoor barrow, out on the downs. Bandits robbing travellers at Hollin Ford. Elsie read them all twice, the way she read everything that mattered. Tamsin read over her head. Tilly read under her arm.

event: Tilly says bandits pay best; Tamsin says bandits fight back.
prose: "Bandits pay best," Tilly said at once, pointing. "Look. Fifteen lanterns. That's five each." She was already doing it on her fingers. "If we did bandits, and then the wolves, and then—" "Bandits fight back," said Tamsin. She said it flatly, and Tilly stopped counting. "Wolves fight back too, but wolves run when it goes against them. Bandits have crossbows, and they don't run, because they'd hang." She looked down at Tilly. "Not bandits. Not yet."

memory.fact: The E-rank bandits notice: bandits robbing travellers at Hollin Ford, fifteen lanterns.

event: Elsie asks about the barrow; Tamsin reads that there are lights and singing there at night.
prose: "What's the barrow?" Elsie asked. "What's a barrow?" "An old grave," Tamsin said. "A hill somebody built over somebody, a long time ago. Out on the downs." She leaned past Elsie and read the notice aloud, squinting at the clerk's small hand. "Bellmoor barrow. Lights seen on the barrow by night, and singing heard. Shepherds afraid to graze it. To be looked into. Ten lanterns." She straightened. "Lights and singing," she said. "At night. On a grave." She made a face. "Ten lanterns for that's cheap."

memory.fact: The E-rank barrow notice: lights and singing by night at Bellmoor barrow, ten lanterns.

event: Elsie says she'd like to know who's singing, and they take the barrow for tomorrow.
prose: Elsie read the notice again. "Singing," she said. She looked round at the others with her eyes shining. "Somebody's singing out there, at night, on a grave, and the shepherds are frightened, and they haven't been up to see who." She touched the paper with one finger. "I'd like to know who's singing," she said. "Wouldn't you? I'd like to know what they're singing about." Tamsin looked at her, and at the notice, and laughed and shook her head. "Course you would," she said. "All right. The barrow." Tilly nodded. "Tomorrow," Elsie said happily. "We'll go tomorrow."

event: The clerk enters the party for Bellmoor barrow, and Cora writes it in her ledger.
prose: They took the notice to the clerk's desk. The clerk, the same thin young woman with ink on her fingers, unpinned it and turned the big book round. She wrote in it: the Fairweather party, for Bellmoor barrow, the fourteenth. She blotted it. Beside Elsie, Cora had opened her ledger on her forearm and was writing the same, in her own small exact hand, at the top of a fresh page: Bellmoor barrow. Lights and singing. The fourteenth. Elsie watched her write it. There was a great deal of empty page under it, waiting.

memory.fact: The Fairweather party took the Bellmoor barrow notice for the fourteenth.

event: Cora says she has her report to write, and goes to the charcoal door.
prose: Cora closed the ledger. "I have my report to write," she said, "on the toll bridge. For the guildmaster." She tucked the ledger under her arm. She looked at Elsie a moment longer, as if there were something else, and then didn't say it. She nodded to Tamsin and Tilly and went across the hall to the charcoal-painted door in the far wall, where the Wardens kept their room. She opened it and went through and shut it behind her. Elsie, watching her go, saw the back of her neck above the collar of her coat. It was still faintly pink.

event: At the Tipsy Heron Tamsin pays for stew for the three of them.
prose: The Tipsy Heron was across the canal from the guild hall, loud and low-beamed and smelling of beer and onions, and at noon it was full of adventurers. Tamsin pushed through them to the counter. Elsie saw her count it out there: twelve copper pips, one after another, out of the purse at her belt and into the tapster's palm. She came back with three bowls of stew balanced along her arms and a loaf tucked under her chin. "My treat," she said, setting them down. "For the bridge. Don't argue." They sat at a scarred table by the window. The stew was thick and brown and full of barley, and very hot.

changes.note: Tamsin buys stew for three at the Tipsy Heron: 12 pips, 184 → 172

event: A tall woman with her arm in a sling sits at the next table: the Hounds' shield-bearer.
prose: A woman came in and sat down at the next table, alone, with a mug. She was tall, taller than Tamsin, broad in the shoulder, with short dark hair and a plain strong face, and her left arm was strapped across her chest in a sling. There was a splint under the sling; Elsie could see the edge of it, and the yellowing bruise at the wrist where it ended. She lowered herself onto the bench carefully, the way people move when a bone is knitting. On the shoulder of her jacket was a stitched badge: a copper hound. Elsie knew whose arm that was before Tamsin had even looked up.

event: Tamsin sees her, goes white, and puts down her spoon.
prose: Tamsin had her spoon halfway to her mouth. She saw the woman. Elsie watched it happen: Tamsin's eyes went to the sling, and to the badge, and to the face, and stopped there. All the colour went out of her. It drained from under her freckles until they stood out like flecks of rust on white, and her green eyes went wide and fixed. Very slowly she put her spoon down in her bowl. She put it down so carefully that it didn't make a sound. Then she sat with her hands flat on the table either side of the bowl and didn't move.

event: Elsie feels it down the Tether, shame like cold water, and puts a hand on Tamsin's knee.
prose: Elsie felt it down the Tether. It came all at once, the way the troll's blow had come, but this didn't ring; it soaked. It was shame, cold and heavy, like being pushed under cold water in her clothes and held there, and it went into her chest and her stomach and her hands until she could hardly breathe for it. She knew it wasn't hers. She knew whose it was. Under the table she reached across and put her hand on Tamsin's knee, flat and warm, and left it there. She didn't say anything. She only held on. Under her palm, through the worn cloth, she could feel Tamsin's leg shaking.

changes.note: Bond: Tamsin 62 → 65 (held through a fear: the shield-bearer; chapter cap of 5)

event: Tamsin gets up, walks to the shield-bearer's table, and stands there.
prose: Tamsin's hand came down over Elsie's under the table and gripped it, hard, once. Then she let go and stood up. Her chair scraped. She walked the three steps to the next table, stiffly, like someone walking out onto ice, and stopped beside it. She stood there. The shield-bearer looked up from her mug. Tamsin stood in front of her with her arms hanging at her sides and her fists opening and closing, and in all the noise of the Heron, the clatter and the shouting and somebody singing badly by the fire, the two of them were perfectly still.

event: She says she's sorry about the arm, and should have said so a week ago.
prose: "I'm sorry about your arm," Tamsin said. Her voice was rough. She cleared her throat and said it again, louder, so it would carry. "I'm sorry about your arm. I should've said so a week ago. At the time. Before they took you off to be set." She swallowed. "I should've come and found you. I didn't. I kept away." Her fists had stopped opening and closing. They hung. "That's all," Tamsin said. "I'm sorry. I'm not asking you for anything. I just should've said it."

event: The shield-bearer looks at her a long time, then says she heard about the wolves and the Tether.
prose: The shield-bearer looked at her. She looked at her a long time, up from the bench, her plain strong face not giving anything away, until Elsie, watching from the next table with her heart going hard, wanted to get up herself. Then the woman set her mug down. "I heard," she said slowly, "about the wolves. In the Glasswood. You in the red, with the wolves all round, and the little pink Enthraller behind you, and you didn't turn on her." She looked past Tamsin, at Elsie. "Heard about the Tether too. The whole hall did."

event: She says it was the red, not Tamsin, and she knows the difference now, and holds out her good hand.
prose: She looked back at Tamsin. "It was the red broke my arm," she said. "Not you. I didn't know that then. I thought it was you, and I said so, to the Hounds and to anyone who'd stand still for it." She shifted the sling against her chest. "I know the difference now," she said. And she held out her good hand, her right, open, across the gap between them. "Reyes," she said.

memory.fact: Tamsin said sorry to the Hounds' shield-bearer, who said the red broke her arm, not Tamsin.
Tamsin said sorry to the Hounds' shield-bearer, who said the red broke her arm, not Tamsin.

event: Tamsin shakes it, and comes back to the table blinking hard.
prose: Tamsin looked at the hand. Then she took it. She shook it, once, hard, the way she'd shake on a bargain, held on a moment longer than the shake needed, and let go. The shield-bearer nodded and went back to her mug. Tamsin turned round and came back to their table. She sat down. She picked up her spoon and put it down again. Her eyes were very bright and she was blinking hard, fast, over and over, looking fixedly at her stew, her mouth pressed shut and working at the corners.

event: Elsie hugs her round the middle, and Tilly hugs them both.
prose: Elsie got up and went round the table and put her arms round Tamsin's middle from the side, as far as they would go, and pressed her face into Tamsin's shoulder and held on. Tamsin made a small sound. Her arm came round Elsie's back, heavy, and her hand closed on a fistful of Elsie's top. Then there was a scrape and a rush, and Tilly was there too, coming round the other side and flinging her arms round the pair of them, squeezing so hard that Elsie's cheek squashed against Tamsin's collarbone and she could feel Tamsin's heart going under it, fast. "You were so brave," Tilly said, muffled, into somebody. "Tamsin. You were so brave."

event: They walk to Willow Canal; the card is still in the blue-doored house's window.
prose: After lunch they walked to Willow Canal. It was a quiet canal, green and narrow, with willows trailing in it and a little hump-backed bridge, and the house was where it had been: narrow and tall, three storeys, its garden gone wild against the railings, its door blue. Elsie walked faster when she saw it. The card was still in the front window. TO LET, it said, in faded copperplate, and under it the agent's name on Coin Street. Elsie stood at the railings with her hands round the bars and looked at it the way she looked at Sunny when he put out a new leaf.

memory.fact: A narrow three-storey house with a blue door and a wild garden is to let on Willow Canal.
The blue-door house on Willow Canal is let through a letting agent on Coin Street.

event: Elsie works out on her fingers what they've saved against what the agent wants, and sighs.
prose: She worked it out on her fingers. She had done it before, in bed at night, but she did it again, because sometimes it came out different. Her own lanterns. Tamsin's. Tilly's. What the barrow would bring. She counted, moving her lips, ran out of fingers, and started again on the first hand. Four suns, the agent wanted, in gold, a month in hand. She came to the end of her counting and looked at her fingers, and then at the blue door, and sighed, a long sigh that went all the way down to her boots.

memory.fact: The blue-door house on Willow Canal needs a month in hand: four suns in gold to start.

event: Tamsin says the barrow pays ten lanterns; Tilly says that's still a great many barrows.
prose: "The barrow's ten lanterns," Tamsin said, leaning on the railings beside her. "That's something. That's a start." Tilly was counting on her own fingers, her lips moving too. She got to the end of them and looked at the house, and at her hands, and back at the house. "That's still a great many barrows," she said in a small voice. "A great many. Is Lanternmere full of barrows? I don't think it is." She looked so stricken that Elsie laughed, and Tamsin laughed, and Tilly, after a moment, laughed too, a little wobbly.

event: Elsie kisses two fingers and presses them to the blue door.
prose: Elsie opened the gate. It squeaked. She went up the short path through the long grass and the poppies and the bindweed to the step, and stood in front of the blue door. Its paint was cracked, and the knocker was a brass hand holding a ball. She kissed two of her fingers and pressed them to the door, flat, in the middle of the blue, and held them there a moment. "Wait for us," she told it softly. Behind her at the railings Tamsin had gone quiet, and Tilly had both hands clasped under her chin.

event: Tilly goes home to brew for the barrow, hugging Elsie twice.
prose: At the corner where Willow Canal met the wider water, Tilly stopped. "I have to brew," she said. "For the barrow. If there's singing, there might be—I don't know what there might be. I need to brew for not knowing." She hugged Elsie, quick and tight, let go and went three steps, then turned round and came back and hugged her again, harder, with her face in Elsie's shoulder and a braid in Elsie's mouth. "Bye," she said into Elsie's top. Then she let go and set off up the towpath toward Pickle Row at a run, her vials clinking.

event: Tamsin walks Elsie home, saying she'll write to Nell about the shield-bearer tonight.
prose: Tamsin walked her home. They went along the canals in the hot early afternoon, slowly, with Margery on Tamsin's shoulder and the unlit lanterns swaying a little over their heads in the breeze. Tamsin was quiet a long time. Then she said, "I'm going to write to Nell tonight. About today. About the shield-bearer." She looked straight ahead. "She'll want to know. They'll be up past the lock by now, but the wharf office sends on." She was quiet again. "I'll tell her I said sorry," she said. "She'll like that."

event: At the Honeycomb door Tamsin hugs her and goes off toward the wharf office.
prose: At the Honeycomb's door Tamsin stopped. She stood looking at Elsie a moment, with the warm bread smell coming out round them, and her face did something complicated. Then she leaned Margery against the wall and hugged her. She hugged her hard, both arms round her, lifting her a little off the step, with her chin on top of Elsie's head and her cheek against Elsie's hair, and held her like that longer than a hug usually went. She set her down. "Tomorrow," Tamsin said. She picked up Margery and went off along Thimble Canal toward the wharf office, and didn't look back.

event: In the attic Elsie writes Tilly's favourite things, leaving a gap for the secret one.
prose: Up in the attic it was warm and close and smelled of bread. Elsie opened the round window over the canal and sat on the end of her bed with her notebook on her knees. She turned to Tilly's page. She had scribbled it on the road; now she wrote it out again, properly, in her best round hand. Pear fizz (her own, not the shop's). Blue flames, the steady kind. The smell of sulphur. Then she left a gap, a good-sized one, three ruled lines of white paper. At the start of the gap she drew a very small question mark, and beside it a very small star.

event: Under Cora she writes: tea, black, one sugar; lavender.
prose: She turned to Cora's page. There wasn't much on it yet: CORA at the top, and under it the two words she had scrawled on the riverbank while Cora wasn't looking round. She wrote them out properly beneath. Tea, black, strong, one sugar. She looked at that. Then, on the line below, slowly, taking care over each letter, she wrote: lavender. She sat and looked at the word a while. She thought of Cora walking beside her on the bank, not looking round, saying it so quietly she'd nearly missed it. She thought of the coat. She found she was smiling at the page.

event: Downstairs she asks the baker where to buy wool, and the baker says Spindle Lane.
prose: Downstairs the shop was quiet, the afternoon loaves cooling on the racks and Agnes behind the counter sorting pips into piles. Elsie leaned on the counter. "Agnes," she said, "where do I buy wool? Good wool, for gloves. Soft." Agnes didn't look up from her pips. "Spindle Lane," she said. "Go to the one with the green shutters, not the one with the cat. The one with the cat cheats." She pushed a pile of pips along the counter. "Gloves," she said. "In summer." "They're for Cora," Elsie said. "Her hands are cold." Agnes looked up at that, and looked at her for a long moment, and grunted.

event: On Spindle Lane Elsie buys grey wool, the grey of Cora's eyes, and pays for it.
prose: Spindle Lane was narrow and cool and smelled of sheep and dye, every shopfront hung with skeins: reds and golds and blues, lavender, moss. Elsie went into the one with the green shutters and along the shelves inside, touching. There was a great deal of grey, and none of it was right, and then one was. It was a soft, cool, pale grey, like the Mere at dawn under its mist, and she held the skein up to the window and knew it at once: it was the grey of Cora's eyes. She took it to the counter. She counted four copper pips out of her purse, one at a time, into the woman's hand.

event: She buys knitting needles too, and pays for those.
prose: "And needles, please," Elsie said. The woman brought out a tray of them, and Elsie chose a pair of smooth, pointed ones of polished birch, not too thick, good for fine work, for fingers. She tried the points against her thumb and smiled. She counted three more pips into the woman's palm, and the purse at her belt hung a little lighter. She came out into Spindle Lane with the grey wool held against her chest in both arms and the needles poking out of her satchel, humming.

changes.note: A pair of knitting needles: 3 pips, 172 → 169
Elsie ends the chapter with 169 pips: 16 lanterns, 9 pips
Tamsin ends the chapter with 172 pips

memory.fact: On Spindle Lane a pair of knitting needles costs three pips.
On Spindle Lane a pair of knitting needles costs three pips.

event: At the round window she casts on the first glove, humming.
prose: She sat on the sill of the round window with her back against the frame and her boots up on the bed, the canal going by below in the late gold light. She wound the skein into a ball first, on her knee, round and round, and then she cast on. She did it the way her mother had shown her by a caravan fire, looping the grey wool over the birch, stitch after stitch, counting under her breath. She thought about Cora's hand: long and narrow and cold in hers in the dark. She made the cuff a little longer than she would have for herself, for those wrists. Somewhere in the counting she had begun to hum.

memory.fact: Elsie is knitting Cora gloves of grey wool, the grey of Cora's eyes, for her cold hands.
Elsie is knitting Cora gloves of grey wool, the grey of Cora's eyes, for her cold hands.
Elsie is knitting Cora gloves of grey wool, the grey of Cora's eyes, for her cold hands.

event: Moonpenny sits beside her on the sill, closed up for the day.
prose: Moonpenny sat beside her on the sill in its little clay pot. It was closed up for the day, its leaves folded, its one fat bud wrapped tight round itself like a fist, waiting for its night. Elsie told it about the guildmaster while she knitted. She told it about the shield-bearer, and Tamsin's face. "And Cora likes lavender," she told it. "I didn't know that. Well. I did, sort of, because of her coat. But I didn't know I knew." Moonpenny, being an orchid, kept its opinions to itself. Below the sill the rest of her plants sat in their crate, and Captain the mint smelled of mint in the warm.

event: The lamplighters' boats come by at dusk, and Elsie has a cuff done.
prose: The light went gold, and then rose, and then blue. The lamplighters' boats came along Thimble Canal at dusk: long narrow boats poled slowly down the middle of the water, a lamplighter standing in the bow of each with a long brass pole and a flame at its tip. They reached up to each paper lantern as they passed, and it bloomed red or gold, one after another, all down the canal, its light dropping onto the water in long shaking stripes. Elsie stopped to watch them. When she looked down at her needles again, she had a cuff done: a neat grey ribbed cuff, the length of her hand.

event: She sees Cora walking alone along Thimble Canal again, and waves.
prose: It was full dark, the lanterns all lit, when she saw her. A figure on the far bank of Thimble Canal, walking alone under the lanterns, coming this way. Elsie knew the walk at once, the way she had known it two nights ago: the straight back, the long even stride, the charcoal coat. Cora, walking along Thimble Canal again, alone, at night. Elsie put her knitting down, leaned out of the round window and waved, with her whole arm, over her head.

event: Cora looks up and lifts her hand at once this time.
prose: Cora looked up. She looked straight up the front of the Honeycomb to the round window, as if she had known exactly where to look. And this time she didn't stop and stand. She lifted her hand at once. She lifted it high, open, palm out, the way she had held it toward the troll under the bridge, except that there was no storm in the air round it now. It was only a hand, raised to Elsie in the lantern light. Elsie, leaning out over the sill with her elbows on the warm stone, felt her whole face go into a smile.

event: Elsie holds up the grey cuff on its needles; Cora tilts her head, puzzled, and walks on.
prose: Elsie snatched up her knitting and held it out of the window for Cora to see: the grey cuff on its birch needles, the ball of wool dangling under it on its strand, turning in the air. She waggled it. She pointed at it, and then down at Cora, and then held it up higher. Down on the far bank, under a red lantern, Cora stood with her hand still half raised and looked up at it. She tilted her head slowly to one side, the way the young troll had tilted his at Tilly's squeak, and looked at it a long moment, puzzled. Then she lowered her hand and walked on along the canal.

event: Elsie writes her mother about the guildmaster laughing, the house, and the gloves.
prose: Later she lit the candle stub on the little table, pulled up the stool and wrote to her mother. Dear Mum, she wrote. Today the guildmaster laughed. She is a swordswoman and Cora says she doesn't laugh, and I told her about the blue-door house, and she laughed with her hand over her eyes. Cora says that's a good sign. Tamsin says so too. The house is still to let. We are a great many barrows away from it, Tilly says. I am knitting gloves for Cora, grey ones, because her hands are cold at night. I have done one cuff. I love you. Elsie.

event: Down the Tether Tamsin feels lighter than Elsie has ever felt her, and Elsie smiles at the ceiling.
prose: She blew out the candle and lay down on her narrow bed in the dark, with the lantern light off the canal moving faintly on the sloped ceiling over her, and folded her hands on her stomach. Down the Tether, from somewhere out along the canals, from Tamsin, came a feeling she had to lie very still to make out. It was lightness. It wasn't happiness exactly, or not only; it was the way a pack feels when it has been carried all day and is set down at last, and the back that carried it straightens and finds itself still there. There was no cold water in it anywhere. Elsie lay and felt it, and smiled at the ceiling.

changes.note: Bond: Tamsin 65 → 66 (Tether: lighter than ever at day's end)
